newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Interior Minister slams U.S. on drugs.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Interior Minister slams U.S. on drugs.

text.p: Interior Minister Horacio Serpa accused the United States on Monday of making Colombia out to be a villain in the drugs war while it sought to cover up its own drug-related problems at home.

Serpa, who recent polls show would be the front-running candidate to succeed President Ernesto Samper in elections next year, was responding to last week's criticism of Colombia by U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard.
In testimony on Capitol Hill in the run-up to the annual U.S. "certification" process, Gelbard called Samper "a truly corrupt president who has had a clear history of co-operating with drug dealers."
Gelbard, who heads the State Department's international narcotics and law enforcement affairs bureau, said Colombia was producing more cocaine and heroin than ever before.

Serpa, who branded Gelbard "rude and brazen," said he had been "totally and absolutely unobjective" in his assessment of Colombia's efforts to fight drugs. The United States had failed to win its own drugs war "since marijuana plantations continue to get bigger in Arizona and California and (drug) consumption continues to increase," Serpa said.
"In order to cover up his own ineptitude, his failures, and to cover up the incapacity of the United States, he (Gelbard) is creating scandals involving Colombia and the Colombian people."

Serpa, Samper's right-hand man, has clashed with the United States frequently. He drew fire from Washington in September 1995 when he suggested U.S. anti-drug agents may have played a role in an assassination attempt on Samper's lawyer and has been Samper's staunchest defender in Congress.

In a related development, Bogota's El Espectador newspaper predicted U.S. President Bill Clinton would "decertify" Colombia for a second consecutive year because of its alleged failure to crack down hard enough on the drug trade.

Clinton is to announce on Feb. 27 whether Colombia should be "certified" as a trustworthy ally in the drugs war. A second consecutive decertification could trigger economic sanctions Clinton fell short of imposing in 1996.
El Espectador said the decision would be prompted more by the Clinton administration's dislike of Samper than by any objective facts.

The newspaper, a frequent critic of Samper, has urged him repeatedly to step down because of his alleged ties to drug lords who contributed up to $6 million to his 1994 campaign. But it said too many Colombians have suffered on the front lines of the drugs war and died in acts of "heroism and martyrdom" for anyone to claim Colombia was "soft" on drugs.
